name: Battle of Crécy

sides.name: Kingdom of England
sides.commander: Edward III, Edward the Black Prince
sides.strength: Roughly 14,000 including about 7,000 longbowmen, 2,500 men-at-arms, and Welsh and Cornish infantry

sides.name: Kingdom of France
sides.strength: Around 30,000 including 12,000 men-at-arms and 6,000 Genoese crossbowmen
sides.casualties: Around 4,000 men-at-arms killed including the Count of Alençon, the King of Bohemia, and several thousand foot

summary: Edward III drew up on a sloping field at Crécy after a long retreat across northern France, placing his dismounted men-at-arms in three divisions and his longbowmen on the wings. The French vanguard arrived disorganised at the end of a long march. A rain shower softened the bowstrings of the Genoese crossbowmen, who advanced anyway and were shot down. The French knights then charged through their own retreating crossbows into a storm of arrows. Fifteen separate charges came in across the late afternoon and into the night. None reached the English line intact.
significance: The English longbow announced itself as the dominant battlefield weapon of the age, and the social order of mounted chivalry began its century-long decline. Crécy made the reputation of the Black Prince, who reportedly received his "spurs" on the field as a sixteen-year-old. It opened the way to Calais and a foothold the English would hold for two hundred years. Together with Poitiers and Agincourt it became the foundational legend of English military exceptionalism.
